abstract: |
 Automated vision models turn video into dense time series of classifier-output scores for visible expression. Dynamic analyses of those scores need a measurement check: a recovery method should find the latent organization that generated the score channels after accounting for the observation process. We introduce the Latent Oscillator Measurement Model (LOMM), a simulation framework that generates latent oscillator trajectories, gates their activity over time, and maps them through block loadings into noisy score channels. LOMM varies latent dimensionality, feedback regime, activity pattern, loading strength, and measurement error. We first calibrated selected temporal and dimensional score-series targets against MAFW-derived classifier-output panels. The softmax-linked realism panel reproduced several local temporal and effective-dimensionality features, but the simulated channels remained more dispersed than the empirical panels. We then tested known-truth recovery on pre-link linear block-measurement panels. In a broad DynEGA grid and a matched comparison with GraphicalVAR and GIMME, DynEGA gave the most consistent dimensional and block recovery in these LOMM simulation designs and completed the broad grid. GraphicalVAR often recovered dimensionality but was slower and more sensitive to weak measurement conditions. GIMME had substantial runtime and completion limits in this design. LOMM gives method researchers a controlled setting for testing whether dynamic recovery methods can recover latent score organization before classifier-output score dynamics are interpreted substantively.

# Introduction

Video is increasingly used as a source of intensive behavioral data because it preserves the temporal ordering of visible action and can be analyzed at a resolution that manual frame-by-frame coding cannot sustain. Deep-learning systems can now convert frames or short video segments into dense time series of model-derived emotional-expression scores [@meng2017IdentityAware; @li2022Deep]. In a facial-expression recognition task, a model maps each image or segment to category probabilities or continuous scores for labels such as happiness, anger, sadness, fear, surprise, disgust, or neutral expression.

These score streams are valuable because many behavioral questions concern how visible affect unfolds over time. Researchers may ask whether expressive states persist or switch, whether they return after perturbation, and whether many model-output channels reflect a smaller number of expressive dimensions. Such questions arise in psychotherapy, autism assessment, collaborative work, public communication, and social-media video [@halamovaAutomatedFacialExpression2023; @holidayMultimodalEmotionPerspective2023; @liDecodingGroupEmotional2024; @manelisbaramComparingThreeAlgorithms2025].

Automated facial-analysis systems now make this kind of work feasible at scale. Datasets such as FER2013 supported deep learning approaches to facial-expression recognition, especially Convolutional Neural Networks [CNNs\; @goodfellow2013Challenges; @arriaga2017Realtimea; @ezerceli2022Convolutional]. Most early systems inherited their emotion categories from the training data and focused on fixed classification tasks, commonly returning probabilities for seven categories: anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness, surprise, and neutral facial expression [@wang2022Rethinking]. More recently, CLIP-based and related vision-language models have enabled zero-shot classification with user-specified emotion labels [@radford2021LearningTransferable; @foteinopoulou2023EmoCLIP; @li2023CLIPER; @tomasevic2026TransforEmotion], making it possible to represent each video frame as a vector of prompt-defined classifier scores.

The main obstacle is measurement. Emotional-expression scores are trained-model outputs that index visible expressive behavior through a scoring procedure. Facial-expression technologies can be interpreted as tools for emotion recognition or social-interaction analysis, and those interpretations answer different questions [@mckeownAreFacialExpression2024]. A separate psychometric question is whether multiple score channels should be treated as variables in their own right or as fallible indicators of lower-dimensional expressive processes [@russellCoreAffect2003; @mehu2015Emotion; @nesselroade2013dynamic]. Measurement error can alter the structure recovered by dynamic methods, so method validation must separate latent temporal organization from the observation process used to measure it [@kankaanpaa2026multipleindicator].

The remaining methodological gap is practical. Researchers need a generator in which latent expressive dynamics and the multichannel observation process are known before any recovery method is applied. Oscillator models describe level, rate of change, damping, and perturbation in intraindividual dynamics [@boker2002Method; @boker2015Adaptive; @ollero2023Characterizing]. A useful validation design must vary dimensionality, indicator blocks, measurement quality, and dynamic regime while keeping the recovery target known.

This paper introduces the Latent Oscillator Measurement Model (LOMM), a generative simulation model for model-derived emotional-expression score channels. LOMM first generates latent expressive trajectories from second-order oscillator dynamics and then maps those latent processes into classifier-output score channels through an explicit measurement layer. The model lets researchers control latent dimensionality, feedback regime, loading strength, measurement error, and activity pattern before testing whether dynamic methods recover the generating structure.

LOMM integrates several established modeling ideas in one inspectable generator. Latent differential-equation models represent level and velocity, continuous-time state-space models motivate the exact transition between observation times, dynamic factor models motivate a multivariate process representation, and the measurement layer separates latent trajectories from fallible observed indicators [@boker2002Method; @boker2015Adaptive; @nesselroade2002; @nesselroade2008dfm]. The network-recovery task then supplies a known indicator partition against which fitted structures can be evaluated. The contribution is this explicit bridge from latent dynamics through classifier-output measurement to structural recovery; the individual oscillator, state-space, factor-model, and graph-estimation components retain their established interpretations.


## The Latent Oscillator Measurement Model

LOMM starts from a measurement object: a video produces frame-level classifier-output score channels for visible expression. The simulation treats those channels as fallible indicators of lower-dimensional expressive processes. A short clip can contain low expressivity, brief expressive episodes, gradual recovery, persistent activation, or alternation between expressive regimes. The latent representation therefore needs to describe level, rate of change, return toward equilibrium, overshoot, damping, and perturbation, concepts that are central to affective-dynamics research [@kuppensEmotionDynamics2017; @houbenRelationShorttermEmotion2015; @hollensteinStateSpaceGrids2007].

Oscillator models provide a compact language for those features. Prior work has used second-order oscillator representations to describe intraindividual dynamics in which a current level and its rate of change jointly determine subsequent movement [@boker2002Method; @boker2015Adaptive; @ollero2023Characterizing]. LOMM uses the same state representation for multivariate simulation and measurement evaluation. It combines three layers: a latent oscillator layer that generates expressive trajectories, an activity layer that controls which latent dimension is expressed over time, and a block measurement layer adapted from direct autoregressive factor-score modeling [@nesselroade2013dynamic; @golino2020modeling].

The latent layer treats each expressive dimension as a second-order state process advanced in discrete simulation steps. For state $\mathbf{s}_{if,t}=[x_{if,t},v_{if,t}]^\top$, the implemented exact linear step is

\begin{equation}
\mathbf{s}_{if,t+dt}
=
\boldsymbol{\Phi}_f(dt)\mathbf{s}_{if,t}
+
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_f(dt)q_{if,t},
\qquad
q_{if,t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{qf}^{2}),
\label{eq:lomm-latent}
\end{equation}

where

$$
\boldsymbol{\Phi}_f(dt)=\exp(\mathbf{A}_f dt),
\qquad
\mathbf{A}_f=
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & 1 \\
\eta_f & \zeta_f
\end{bmatrix}
\qquad
\text{and}
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_f(dt)=\int_0^{dt}\exp(\mathbf{A}_f u)\mathbf{b}\,du,
\quad
\mathbf{b}=
\begin{bmatrix}
0 \\
1
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

For the nonzero position-feedback values used in the simulation grids, the input map has the equivalent exact form

$$
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_f(dt)
=\mathbf{A}_f^{-1}\{\boldsymbol{\Phi}_f(dt)-\mathbf{I}_2\}\mathbf{b}.
$$

The integral definition remains valid at singular parameter values and supplies the continuous limit used by the implementation near repeated roots.

In Equation \ref{eq:lomm-latent}, $i$ indexes videos, $f$ indexes latent expressive dimensions, and $t$ indexes discrete simulation time points spaced $dt$ apart. The state variable $x_{if,t}$ is the latent level of dimension $f$ for video $i$, and $v_{if,t}$ is its rate of change. The parameter $\eta_f$ is position feedback, $\zeta_f$ is velocity feedback, $q_{if,t}$ is the stepwise Gaussian acceleration input used at each transition, and $\sigma_{qf}$ is the standard deviation of that input. Within a step, the recursion is the exact transition of the linear second-order oscillator $\ddot{x}_{if}=\eta_f x_{if}+\zeta_f \dot{x}_{if}+q_{if,t}$ with the shock held constant, so $\boldsymbol{\Phi}_f(dt)$ propagates the deterministic state and $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_f(dt)$ is the zero-order-hold loading through which $q_{if,t}$ enters as a per-step acceleration input.

The dynamic parameters set the latent regime. The characteristic roots for factor $f$ are

$$
r_{f,\pm}=\frac{\zeta_f\pm\sqrt{\zeta_f^2+4\eta_f}}{2}.
$$

Continuous-time asymptotic stability requires $\eta_f<0$ and $\zeta_f<0$, and the roots are oscillatory when $\zeta_f^2+4\eta_f<0$. The exact discrete transition is asymptotically stable when

$$
\rho\{\boldsymbol{\Phi}_f(dt)\}
=\exp\!\left[dt\max\{\operatorname{Re}(r_{f,+}),\operatorname{Re}(r_{f,-})\}\right]<1.
$$

Negative $\eta_f$ supplies restoring acceleration, negative $\zeta_f$ attenuates velocity, and positive $\zeta_f$ produces anti-damped amplification over a finite interval. For a sequence with $T$ observations, the observed horizon is $H=(T-1)dt$, and the corresponding deterministic growth diagnostic is $g_f(H)=\exp\{H\max\operatorname{Re}(r_{f,+},r_{f,-})\}$. Reporting $T$, $dt$, $H$, the roots, and $g_f(H)$ distinguishes stable oscillation, gated nonstationarity, and finite-horizon amplification.

The model uses an uncoupled multivariate system: $\eta_f$, $\zeta_f$, and $\sigma_{qf}$ may vary by factor, and off-diagonal dynamic effects are omitted. The checked-in simulations initialized every factor at $x_{if,1}=0.25$ and $v_{if,1}=2$. The revised robustness protocol uses independent starting states. For a stable factor, it solves

$$
\mathbf{P}_f=\boldsymbol{\Phi}_f\mathbf{P}_f\boldsymbol{\Phi}_f^\top
+\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_f\sigma_{qf}^2\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_f^\top
$$

and draws $\mathbf{s}_{if,1}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{P}_f)$. For an anti-damped factor, it draws $x_{if,1}\sim\mathrm{Unif}(-0.25,0.25)$ and $v_{if,1}\sim\mathrm{Unif}(-2,2)$. These independent starts remove the common deterministic transient from the revised sensitivity design while leaving the observed horizon unchanged.
<!-- REVISION_RESULTS_PENDING[challenge_dynega,challenge_graphicalvar,challenge_static_oracle]; CLAIM_LEDGER[clm-v2-measurement-challenges]: Replace the checked-in initialization comparison with paired estimates after all three challenge manifests validate. -->

The activity layer turns raw oscillator states into scenario-specific expression episodes. The trajectory passed to the measurement model is $\tilde{x}_{if,t}=a_{if,t}x_{if,t}$, where $a_{if,t}\geq 0$ is a scenario-defined activity envelope generated from active gains, background gains, and dwell schedules. Its derivative contains both oscillator motion and gate motion,

$$
\frac{d}{dt}\{a_{if}(t)x_{if}(t)\}
=a_{if}'(t)x_{if}(t)+a_{if}(t)x_{if}'(t).
$$

For the piecewise-constant schedules used in the checked-in simulations, the corresponding finite-difference identity is

$$
\frac{\tilde{x}_{if,t+dt}-\tilde{x}_{if,t}}{dt}
=a_{if,t+dt}\frac{x_{if,t+dt}-x_{if,t}}{dt}
+\frac{a_{if,t+dt}-a_{if,t}}{dt}x_{if,t}.
$$

In single-regime scenarios, one dimension has higher activity across the full sequence; in switching scenarios, the active dimension changes after sampled dwell intervals; and in low-expression scenarios, all dimensions remain close to background activity. Abrupt gates can introduce a derivative signal at a switch even when oscillator acceleration is unchanged. The revised challenge design therefore compares the checked-in step gates with five-observation half-cosine transitions while preserving the generating dimensions and indicator memberships.
<!-- REVISION_RESULTS_PENDING[challenge_dynega,challenge_graphicalvar,challenge_static_oracle]; CLAIM_LEDGER[clm-v2-measurement-challenges]: Insert the paired smooth-gate sensitivity after all three challenge manifests validate. -->

The measurement layer maps the activity-scaled latent trajectories into simulated score channels. For video $i$, if each latent dimension has $k$ observed indicators, then the number of observed score channels is $p=mk$ and the linear score vector is

\begin{equation}
\mathbf{z}_{it}=\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_i\,\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{it}+\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{it},
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{it}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i).
\label{eq:lomm-measurement}
\end{equation}

In Equation \ref{eq:lomm-measurement}, $\mathbf{z}_{it}$ is the $p$-channel linear score vector, $\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{it}$ is the $m$-dimensional activity-scaled latent vector, $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_i$ is a $p\times m$ loading matrix, $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{it}$ is measurement error, and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i$ is the error covariance matrix. Each observed score belongs to one indicator block $B_f$ and loads on exactly one latent dimension: for indicator $j$ in block $B_f$, $(\Lambda_i)_{jf}=\lambda+u_{ij}$ with baseline loading $\lambda$ and loading jitter $u_{ij}\sim\mathrm{Unif}(-0.15,0.15)$; all off-block loadings are zero. The measurement-error covariance matrix is diagonal, $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i=\mathrm{diag}(\sigma^2_{\varepsilon,i1},\ldots,\sigma^2_{\varepsilon,ip})$, with $\sigma^2_{\varepsilon,ij}=s^2_{\varepsilon}+r_{ij}$ and item-level variance jitter $r_{ij}\sim\mathrm{Unif}(-0.01,0.01)$. The simulation grid reports $s_{\varepsilon}$ as the measurement-error standard deviation, and $s^2_{\varepsilon}$ enters the covariance matrix before item-level jitter is added on the variance scale.

These observed channels are classifier-output measurements of visible expression. The block model tests whether recovery methods recover a prespecified observation process under controlled loading strength, measurement error, dynamic regime, and activity regime. It leaves semantic label validity and subjective emotional experience outside the evidential scope of the simulation.

For the empirical realism check, the linear score vector is transformed to a bounded observed scale with a row-wise softmax link. If $\mathbf{z}_{it}$ is the pre-link score vector from Equation \ref{eq:lomm-measurement}, the general link is

$$
y_{itj}=\frac{\exp\{(\alpha_j+z_{itj})/\tau\}}
{\sum_{r=1}^{p}\exp\{(\alpha_r+z_{itr})/\tau\}},
\qquad \tau>0,
$$

with centered channel intercepts satisfying $\sum_j\alpha_j=0$. The checked-in realism layer used $\boldsymbol{\alpha}=\mathbf{0}$ and $\tau=1$. The softmax is invariant to a common shift of every logit, and its unit-sum constraint induces dependence among observed channels. Temperature also trades off against the scale of the logits. The empirical realism analysis uses the bounded $\mathbf{y}_{it}$ panel, whereas the checked-in dimensional-recovery simulations use the linear $\mathbf{z}_{it}$ panel. The revised bounded-score sensitivity evaluates raw probabilities and centered log-ratios while retaining the generating blocks at the logit measurement layer. Neutral can appear as an empirical classifier-output channel, but it is not assigned a source-truth latent factor unless a neutral block is specified by design.
<!-- REVISION_RESULTS_PENDING[empirical_cv,challenge_dynega,challenge_graphicalvar,challenge_static_oracle]; CLAIM_LEDGER[clm-v2-held-out-realism,clm-v2-measurement-challenges]: Replace the fixed-link description with fold-selected training-only intercept and temperature estimates, then report raw-probability and CLR recovery after the corresponding manifests validate. -->

As an illustrative substantive mapping, a three-factor LOMM could represent approach-affiliation, threat-defense, and orienting-novelty dimensions. Prompt-defined classifier-output channels related to happiness, amusement, trust, or smiling could form an approach-affiliation block. Channels related to anger, fear, disgust, contempt, or anxiety could form a threat-defense block. Channels related to surprise, anticipation, confusion, or attention could form an orienting-novelty block. These labels are examples for simulation design, not validated affect categories in the empirical MAFW panels. The example draws on affect taxonomies that distinguish broad dimensions, discrete expression families, and opponent tendencies [@russellCircumplexModel1980; @russellCoreAffect2003; @russellMehrabianThreeFactor1977; @plutchikNatureEmotions2001], and it is consistent with facial-expression benchmarks that combine categorical expression labels with dimensional ratings [@mollahosseiniAffectNetDatabase2019; @kolliasABAW2023; @mehu2015Emotion]. Alternative affective taxonomies can be encoded by changing the latent block map while keeping the LOMM architecture fixed.

### Model Scope and Identifiability

The known simulation settings do not imply that every LOMM component can be identified from an empirical score panel. Block labels are recoverable only up to permutation, and latent trajectory signs and scales depend on the chosen constraints. For any nonsingular diagonal matrix $\mathbf{D}$,

$$
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_i\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{it}
=(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_i\mathbf{D}^{-1})(\mathbf{D}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{it}),
$$

so loading magnitude and latent-trajectory scale are not jointly identified without scale constraints. Activity gain and innovation scale also contribute to latent amplitude. The softmax layer adds common-location invariance and a temperature--scale tradeoff. LOMM is used here as a controlled generator with known settings and a prespecified partition target. Empirical use of the framework would require additional scale, loading, and observation-model constraints before its dynamic parameters could be interpreted as estimates.

The same three-factor example is shown in @fig-dlosim to make the role of the latent shock term visible.

The left panel shows smooth reference trajectories without dynamic shocks; the right panel shows trajectories generated by the implemented linear oscillator process with factor-specific position feedback, velocity feedback, and innovation variance."

@fig-dlosim shows the role of the innovation variance, $\sigma_q^2$, in LOMM. The reference panel shows the conceptual latent ordering without dynamic shocks: affiliative expression rises quickly and settles above the threat and orienting trajectories. The simulated oscillator panel retains this ordering while nonzero factor-specific $\sigma_q$ perturbs each latent process at each time point, producing local peaks, reversals, and irregular fluctuations around the underlying trajectory. After approximately time point 100, affiliative expression (blue) remains the dominant latent tendency, while threat (orange) fluctuates at a moderate level and orienting (green) stays lower with shorter local excursions. In this example, $\sigma_q$ turns a smooth conceptual model into latent score series that better resemble uneven temporal structure in model-derived visible-expression panels.


## Present Research

Dynamic Exploratory Graph Analysis [DynEGA; @golino2020modeling] is the focal dynamic-dimensionality estimator because it was developed to recover groups of variables whose estimated changes are coordinated over time. This role supplies a substantive reason to include DynEGA in the design before its performance is known. GraphicalVAR and GIMME provide adjacent intensive-longitudinal pipelines with different estimands and graph-conversion steps, while static EGA evaluates whether temporal preprocessing adds recovery information beyond contemporaneous score levels. A true-block oracle checks the simulation and partition code against the known measurement structure.

The revised study addresses three questions. First, can LOMM reproduce held-out observable properties of empirical video-derived classifier-output scores without allowing clip boundaries or training-derived summaries to enter the evaluation fold? Second, how do DynEGA, GraphicalVAR, GIMME, and static EGA recover the same known block structure on matched panels, and where does the oracle place the implementation ceiling? Third, how does recovery change under short records, alternative initialization and stability regimes, smooth activity transitions, cross-loadings, correlated errors and shocks, bounded score representations, and estimator feasibility limits?

The evaluation begins with five-fold clip-level empirical calibration and a matched method comparison on identical generated panels. The matched design provides the primary evidence because panel keys, simulation seeds, structural targets, and the downstream partition rule are shared across pipelines. A broad DynEGA grid then describes the focal method's wider operating envelope. A separate $T=25$ same-cadence study and a bounded challenge suite evaluate departures that are especially relevant to short classifier-output streams and nonideal measurement. The prepared analyses remain prospective until their run manifests and output hashes validate; the checked-in quantitative Results are retained during this pre-compute revision.

Appendix A gives the population argument that motivates the recovery predictions. Under ideal block measurement, common within-block signal and independent cross-block processes produce separated population components. Weaker loadings, larger measurement error, lower activity, and cross-block dependence reduce the weakest within-block recovery margin. The simulations test these predictions as panel-paired changes while separating usable-output probability from recovery conditional on a usable output.

# Method

The analyses follow the workflow in @fig-pipeline. We first use empirical video-score panels to define selected realism targets for model-derived expression-score series (Panels A--C). We then translate those targets into LOMM scenario conditions (Panel D) and evaluate dimensional-recovery methods on simulated panels whose dimensionality and indicator blocks are specified by the simulation design (Panels E--H).

## Empirical Calibration and Realism Targets

@fig-mafwvideo illustrates the empirical score-series surface used to motivate the simulation study. MAFW, introduced as *MAFW: A Large-scale, Multi-modal, Compound Affective Database for Dynamic Facial Expression Recognition in the Wild*, supplies naturalistic video clips for calibrating selected score-series statistics [@liu_mafw_2022]. The dataset does not validate the classifier-output labels, the scoring model, or the subjective emotional states of the people in the clips. The four frames identify the dataset-derived scoring example. The repository and archive do not include raw MAFW videos, and access to the original video materials remains governed by the dataset providers. The realism check uses a 100-clip calibration sample scored with the same zero-shot procedure as the illustrated clip.

We used the transforEmotion R package to generate frame-level classifier-output scores from the calibration videos [@tomasevic2026TransforEmotion]. The scoring call used model key `oai-large`, which maps in the local model registry to `openai/clip-vit-large-patch14`, corresponding to OpenAI CLIP ViT-Large/14. Each sampled video was decoded into frames and scored against the prompt-defined classifier-output channels labeled anger, disgust, fear, happiness, neutral, sadness, surprise, contempt, anxiety, helplessness, and disappointment. These 11 prompt channels follow the MAFW single-label schema and are model outputs rather than frame-level human annotations. Within each clip, short missing runs were interpolated, frames with complete usable scores were retained, and clipped score vectors were renormalized as probability-like outputs. These prompt-defined classifier-output panels define empirical targets for the LOMM observation layer through their temporal persistence, variability, and co-fluctuation.

The selected frames from the same MAFW clip anchor the empirical example (Panel A). Their classifier-output score profiles show that different frames receive different values across channels labeled helplessness, fear, disgust, sadness, anxiety, and disappointment (Panel B). The frame-level trajectories show that the highest mean channels change in bursts with irregular local movement (Panel C). The single-video DynEGA network partitions the same clip's non-neutral classifier-output trajectories (Panel D). This panel is an illustrative readout of model-output channels in one clip; the simulation study later tests recovery under a prespecified generating structure.

The empirical calibration sample was assembled at the clip level from a label-diverse MAFW manifest, with MAFW category labels used for sample diversity rather than validation targets. After interpolation of short missing runs and complete-row filtering, the retained panel contains 100 clips spanning the 11 MAFW single-label categories. Usable clip lengths ranged from 17 to 50 frames, with a median of 36.5 usable frames. These retained frame-score panels define the empirical distributions used for the realism targets, and the short clip lengths bound the interpretation of autocorrelation and spectral summaries.

For the empirical realism check, empirical and simulated panels are summarized at two levels. Observable-channel metrics are computed directly from the classifier-output score series within each clip. Recovered community-score summaries are computed after applying pooled DynEGA to the score panel and extracting score summaries for the recovered communities. This second readout is method-dependent descriptive information, not independent evidence that the empirical videos contain the same latent dimensions as the simulation. The observable-channel readout evaluates channel-level amplitude and movement; the recovered community-score readout evaluates the lower-dimensional geometry induced by this DynEGA summarization step.

The primary realism targets summarize dispersion, local movement, temporal structure, and effective multivariate dimensionality. Channel IQR is the interquartile range of a score series, so higher values mean wider score dispersion. Derivative IQR is the interquartile range of first differences, so higher values mean larger frame-to-frame movement. Lag-1 autocorrelation indexes local persistence. Run-length entropy is the entropy of monotonic run lengths in the first-difference sign series, so higher values indicate more varied directional regimes. Spectral entropy is the normalized entropy of the fast-Fourier-transform power distribution, so higher values indicate broader spectral complexity. Effective rank is the entropy-based rank of the clip-level correlation matrix, so higher values indicate more effective multivariate dimensionality in the score panel.

For channel IQR, derivative IQR, lag-1 autocorrelation, run-length entropy, and spectral entropy, the empirical and simulated distributions contain one value for each clip-by-channel series or clip-by-community-summary series. For effective rank, the distributions contain one value for each clip panel. For each metric distribution, we compare empirical and simulated values using a scaled median difference and a scaled one-dimensional Wasserstein distance. Both discrepancies are divided by the empirical interquartile range for that metric distribution, with a standard-deviation fallback when the empirical interquartile range is near zero. We describe the larger discrepancy as small when it is at most 0.33 empirical interquartile ranges, intermediate when it is above 0.33 and at most 1.00 interquartile range, and large when it exceeds 1.00 interquartile range. The lower threshold approximates one-third of the empirical interquartile range and preserves the implemented value. These heuristic, scale-relative bands make the magnitude easier to read; the continuous discrepancy and its uncertainty remain the evidential quantities. The bands are neither inferential cutoffs nor validation thresholds for the scoring model or prompt labels.

The prospective realism analysis uses five clip-level folds assigned deterministically within MAFW label and usable-length order. Each fold holds out 20 clips. Softmax channel intercepts, temperature, oscillator calibration, and the secondary DynEGA community summarizer are estimated on the remaining 80 clips and then held fixed. Time-delay embeddings carry clip identifiers, so derivative windows cannot cross a clip boundary. Candidate selection uses the observable-channel discrepancy as its primary loss, while the frozen community-score discrepancy remains secondary. The selected calibration generates 100 evaluation panels for each held-out fold. Clip-level metric contributions are retained for 2,000-resample clip-cluster intervals; no held-out clip contributes to calibration or summarizer estimation.

## Scenario Selection

Scenario selection links the empirical calibration targets to the simulation design. We group manipulated conditions into three parameter families (Panel D). The dynamics family varies the position feedback, velocity feedback, and innovation variance parameters, $\eta_f$, $\zeta_f$, and $\sigma_{qf}$. The activity family varies whether one latent expressive dimension dominates across the full sequence, whether dominance switches after sampled dwell intervals, or whether all dimensions remain close to low-expression background activity. The measurement family varies the block loading matrix $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_i$ and measurement-error covariance matrix $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i$ that generate the observed classifier-output score panels.

The scenario set contains six activity-and-dynamics families. Four families are generic score-panel regimes: low-expression single dominance, high-expression single dominance, high-expression switching, and high-expression rapid switching. Two families use the empirical calibration logic more directly: ranked-persistence and broad switching-geometry. @tbl-scenario-families summarizes the activity envelope and dynamic rules used by each family. Across these families, LOMM varies the latent dimensionality and measurement layer so that the number of observed channels equals the number of latent dimensions times the number of indicators per dimension, $p=mk$. The matched three-method grid uses two- and three-dimensional generating structures, and the broad DynEGA extension includes two-, three-, and four-dimensional structures. The final crossed factors, replication counts, and method-specific grid sizes are specified in the dimensional-recovery simulation section below.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-scenario-families
#| tbl-cap: "Activity-and-dynamics scenario families used in the final simulations. Rows vary expression strength, switching, dwell length, feedback pattern, and innovation scale. Dwell values are fractions of the simulated sequence length."
#| results: asis

scenario_family_table <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Family, ~Source, ~Switching, ~`Active/background gain`, ~`Dwell fraction`, ~`Dynamic rule`,
  "Low-expression single dominance", "Generic score-panel regime", "No", "0.35 / 0.05", "1.00 / 1.00", "Template feedback; low innovation scale",
  "High-expression single dominance", "Generic score-panel regime", "No", "1.00 / 0.08", "1.00 / 1.00", "Template feedback; baseline innovation scale",
  "High-expression switching", "Generic score-panel regime", "Yes", "1.00 / 0.08", "0.20 / 0.45", "Template feedback; baseline innovation scale",
  "High-expression rapid switching", "Generic score-panel regime", "Yes", "1.25 / 0.08", "0.03 / 0.10", "Template feedback; high innovation scale",
  "Ranked-persistence", "Calibration-inspired regime", "No", "1.00 / 0.08", "1.00 / 1.00", "Ranked feedback; moderate innovation scale",
  "Broad switching-geometry", "Calibration-inspired regime", "Yes", "1.10 / 0.10", "0.12 / 0.30", "Ranked feedback; higher innovation scale"
)
cat("\\begingroup\\scriptsize\\setlength{\\tabcolsep}{3pt}\n")
print(knitr::kable(
  scenario_family_table,
  booktabs = TRUE,
  escape = FALSE,
  align = c("l", "l", "c", "c", "c", "l")
))
cat("\\endgroup\n")
```

Numerical values for feedback and innovation-scale settings are reported in the supplementary scenario-parameter tables.

For each simulated video, LOMM first generates latent trajectories from the scenario-specific dynamic parameters. The activity schedule then scales those trajectories. Non-switching scenarios keep one active dimension for the full sequence and rotate the dominant dimension across videos. Switching scenarios sample dwell intervals and change the active dimension over time. The measurement layer is applied to the activity-scaled latent trajectories. Measurement error is reported as a standard deviation, with the corresponding variance entering the diagonal measurement-error covariance before small item-level variance jitter is added. The simulation design evaluates dimensional recovery under controlled combinations of dynamics, activity regimes, and measurement quality.

## Dimensional-Recovery Simulation Study

The simulation begins with latent trajectories and the prespecified number of simulated expressive dimensions (Panel E). The LOMM observation layer maps each observed score channel to one latent dimension through the block loading matrix and adds item-level measurement error (Panel F), producing a pre-link simulated score panel (Panel G). The final step is the dimensional-recovery test, where the estimated number of dimensions and item memberships are compared against the generating measurement structure (Panel H).

The method comparison uses a common graph-partitioning target. Each pipeline receives the same simulated score panel, estimates a structure among observed score channels, converts that structure to communities, and compares the resulting partition with the generating indicator blocks. The target is recovery of LOMM-generated score blocks. Classifier-label validity and method superiority for substantive emotion inference are outside this test.

The matched three-pipeline design is the primary comparative analysis. We compare Dynamic Exploratory Graph Analysis [DynEGA; @golino2020modeling] with GraphicalVAR [@epskampggm; @graphicalVAR2024] and GIMME [@gates2012group; @lane2019uncovering] because they represent adjacent approaches to intensive longitudinal structure. DynEGA is the focal dimensional-recovery method because it estimates groups of variables whose changes are coordinated over time. In the present simulation, DynEGA tests direct recovery of the generating score blocks. GraphicalVAR is a dynamic-network comparator that separates lagged temporal relations from contemporaneous partial associations, and its fitted contemporaneous structure is partitioned after estimation. GIMME is an indirect feasibility-stress comparator: it estimates time-series paths for each clip treated as a separate time series, and the resulting contemporaneous structures are aggregated and partitioned. This use of GIMME treats clips as analytic series and should not be read as participant-level idiographic affect modeling.

DynEGA combines time-delay embedding and derivative estimation from dynamical systems with exploratory graph analysis for dimensionality assessment [@glla2010; @golino2017ega1; @golino2019investigating]. We apply DynEGA to the stacked video panel with video identity supplied as the grouping variable. The embedding dimension is selected by minimizing the Total Entropy Fit Index (TEFI) over candidate values [@golino2019entropy], using $n_\mathrm{embed}\in\{5,10,15,\lfloor T/4\rfloor,\lfloor T/2\rfloor\}$ where admissible. The LOMM generator retains the physical step $dt=0.4$ and uses it to calculate the observed horizon. The EGAnet GLLA call records `delta = 1`, corresponding to one observation interval. Expressing the derivatives per unit of physical time would multiply every channel derivative by the common positive factor $1/dt$; this rescaling leaves the derivative correlation matrix and its downstream EBICglasso network unchanged. The run artifacts record physical `dt` and the DynEGA observation-unit `delta` separately. We explicitly set `model = "glasso"` so DynEGA estimates an EBICglasso regularized partial-correlation network from the pooled derivative panel. That network is partitioned into communities interpreted as recovered groups of score channels. The checked-in broad grid uses Louvain community detection [@blondel2008fast] with the expand rule for unidimensional solutions. The checked-in matched grid reports Louvain, Leiden [@traag2019leiden], and Walktrap [@pons2006walktrap] readouts.
<!-- REVISION_RESULTS_PENDING[t100_dynega]; CLAIM_LEDGER[clm-v2-matched-recovery]: Replace the checked-in DynEGA partition description with the frozen-network common-partition pipeline, then add the expand and correlation-Louvain 0.95 paired sensitivities. -->

GraphicalVAR estimates a graphical vector autoregressive model for intensive longitudinal data [@epskampggm; @graphicalVAR2024]. In this framework, the temporal network contains directed lag-1 regression parameters, and the contemporaneous network contains partial correlations among residuals at the same time point after lagged effects have been taken into account. In multilevel applications, the model can also distinguish within-person temporal and contemporaneous structure from between-person associations among stationary means. We fit GraphicalVAR to the stacked simulated score panel and use the estimated contemporaneous partial-correlation matrix as the structural matrix for dimensional partitioning, because LOMM recovery targets an undirected grouping of score channels. The diagonal is ignored and the resulting weighted matrix is treated as an undirected graph. Positive edge weights define the graph, with absolute weights used only when no positive edges are available. Louvain, Leiden, and Walktrap are applied to the same fitted contemporaneous structure and are analyzed as the community-detection factor.

GIMME is an automated time-series modeling approach built around unified structural equation modeling and vector autoregressive representations [@gates2012group; @lane2019uncovering]. The algorithm searches for lagged and contemporaneous paths that improve fit across the sample, retains paths that are common to many series, and then allows subgroup-shared or series-specific paths. In this simulation, each video clip is treated as the time series supplied to GIMME. We fit the VAR specification to the video-level score panels, extract the contemporaneous block from the clip-specific $\boldsymbol{\Psi}$ matrices, and average those blocks across clips to obtain a common structural matrix for dimensional partitioning. The diagonal is ignored, the matrix is symmetrized, and negative entries are set to zero. A matrix with no remaining positive edge yields singleton communities rather than an absolute-weight fallback. Louvain, Leiden, and Walktrap are applied to the same fitted GIMME structure and are analyzed as the community-detection factor.

The matched grid is the primary comparative design. All three fitted structures are converted to dimensional partitions and evaluated against the same prespecified generating structure. DynEGA is then evaluated on the broader grid to assess scalability across the larger LOMM design space. GraphicalVAR and GIMME are restricted to the matched grid because complete factorial estimation is computationally unstable in this setting. Community detection is a diagnostic factor in the matched design; method and simulation design remain the primary organizing variables. Appendix A derives the population structural signal supplied by each pipeline and collects implementation differences in a common perturbation framework.
<!-- REVISION_RESULTS_PENDING[t100_reuse_audit,t100_dynega]; CLAIM_LEDGER[clm-v2-matched-recovery]: Retain the claim of identical generated panels only after panel_key, seed, scenario, N, T, dt, dimensionality, indicator count, loading, error, and innovation hashes agree across methods. -->

The prospective revision specification locks the matched $T=100$ design to 21,600 generated panels: six scenario families, two generating dimensionalities, two sample sizes, three measurement-error levels, three loading levels, and 100 paired replications. Every method receives a method-independent panel key, paired simulation seed, generator specification hash, observed horizon, and stability classification. DynEGA, GraphicalVAR, GIMME, and static EGA each supply one retained structure per panel; Louvain at resolution 1.0 is the primary common partition, and Leiden and Walktrap are paired sensitivity readouts of that same structure. The true-block oracle passes the generating block matrix through the identical partition helper. DynEGA additionally retains its native expand readout and a correlation-Louvain readout at resolution 0.95 as secondary paired analyses. GIMME's common structural matrix is the positive part of the symmetrized mean contemporaneous matrix, $[(\bar{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}+\bar{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^\top)/2]_+$.

The short-record study repeats the 21,600-panel design with $T=25$, $dt=0.4$, and observed horizon $H=9.6$, using DynEGA embedding candidates $\{5,6,10,12\}$ and seeds paired to the corresponding $T=100$ conditions. It is interpreted as a same-cadence, shorter-horizon stress test. GIMME is designated as outside its preferred design range in this condition, and its 900-second per-panel budget is retained in the feasibility denominator. The separate challenge suite crosses the six scenario families, two dimensionalities, 50 paired replications, and seven one-factor-at-a-time variants. It fixes $N=100$, $T=100$, error standard deviation 0.25, loading 0.60, and four indicators per factor; the variants address initialization, smooth gates, cross-loadings, residual correlation, innovation correlation, and bounded softmax scores represented both raw and by centered log-ratios.

Performance is summarized using dimensional hit rate, assignment accuracy for observed score channels, matched trajectory-recovery correlation, matched trajectory-recovery normalized root mean squared error (NRMSE), runtime, and failure or timeout accounting. Method-readout rows are the denominator for dimensional hit rate and the status counts in @tbl-method-overall; they include one row per method, generated panel, and community-detection readout. For GraphicalVAR and GIMME, feasibility is also reported as unique structure-fit status counts before the repeated Louvain, Leiden, and Walktrap readouts. Dimensional hit rate is the proportion of method-readout rows in which the method returns the correct number of latent dimensions. Assignment accuracy is computed for readouts with available partitions and asks whether observed score channels are assigned to the correct generating blocks after optimal matching of estimated communities to those blocks. For trajectory-recovery metrics, observed variables are standardized within the full panel and recovered community-score summaries are computed from the first principal component of each estimated block, with row means used when a principal-component score cannot be estimated. Matched trajectory-recovery correlation and NRMSE compare these recovered score summaries with the generating latent trajectories after sign-invariant matching between estimated communities and generating dimensions. These trajectory-recovery diagnostics are computed only when score summaries are available; they are secondary diagnostics rather than status-inclusive method-performance measures. Runtime is recorded for each model fit.

The prospective result contract separates estimator feasibility from recovery after a usable output. It reports $P(\mathrm{usable})$, $P(\widehat m=m\mid\mathrm{usable})$, and $P(\mathrm{usable\ and\ correct})$; signed and absolute dimension error; adjusted Rand index, variation of information, and assignment accuracy conditional on a usable partition; marginal score correlation and NRMSE; completion within 900 seconds; restricted compute time $\min(\mathrm{runtime},900)$; and the median and interquartile range of runtime among successful fits. Method, horizon, oracle, and challenge contrasts are panel-paired. Uncertainty uses 2,000 panel-cluster resamples, accompanied by Monte Carlo standard errors. Error, timeout, and partial rows remain in every status-inclusive denominator.

The final simulation uses a split design. The matched three-method grid uses four indicators per latent dimension, two- and three-dimensional generating structures, two sample sizes, 100 time points, three loading strengths, three measurement-error standard deviations, and all six scenario families. The reported final runs fix the innovation quality scale at $Q=0.75$, so the scenario base $\sigma_q$ vectors listed in the supplementary scenario-parameter tables are the final-run innovation vectors. The latent systems were advanced with the exact linear transition of Equation \ref{eq:lomm-latent} using step size $dt=0.4$ for 100-point series and $dt=0.25$ for 300-point series, so $\sigma_{qf}$ is the per-step shock standard deviation at that resolution. This matched grid contains 216 structural cells with 100 replications. Louvain, Leiden, and Walktrap are included as community-detection levels, yielding 64,800 method-readout rows per method in the matched three-method grid. The broad DynEGA extension varies the number of videos, series length, latent dimensionality, indicators per dimension, loading strength, and measurement-error standard deviation across 1,296 structural cells with 400 replications, yielding 518,400 DynEGA Louvain/expand method rows. Timeouts, failed fits, and post-estimation extraction errors are retained in the reporting denominator because they are part of method behavior in applied simulation workflows.

## Computational Environment

Final run metadata records R 4.5.1 on Rocky Linux 8.8 (`x86_64-redhat-linux-gnu`), 48 available logical cores, OpenBLAS 0.3.15, and LAPACK 3.9.0. Local inspection of the execution host for this final-results workspace reports dual Intel Xeon Silver 4310 CPUs, 48 logical threads, and 125 GiB RAM. The run artifacts store the operating system, R session, and available-core count; they do not store RAM or a separate hostname. Key package versions were EGAnet 2.3.0, graphicalVAR 0.3.4, gimme 10.0, igraph 2.2.1, qgraph 1.9.8, psych 2.5.6, lavaan 0.6-20, dplyr 1.1.4, and ggplot2 4.0.1. Parallel jobs used one BLAS thread per worker. The broad DynEGA grid used 16 workers with one internal DynEGA core per fit, the matched DynEGA community-detection supplement used 32 workers, and the GraphicalVAR and GIMME matched-grid runs each used 24 workers with a 900-second elapsed-time limit per structure fit.

Runtime is elapsed wall-clock time, recorded with `proc.time()[["elapsed"]]` for successful fitted structures and summarized in seconds. For GraphicalVAR and GIMME, the recorded runtime includes the structure fit and post-fit extraction/community-detection readout. The same fitted structure is reused for Louvain, Leiden, and Walktrap, so feasibility accounting separates unique structure-fit status from repeated method-readout rows. Runtime summaries use successful fits. Timeout and error rows remain in feasibility and recovery denominators. The runtime results should therefore be read as within-machine feasibility estimates for this simulation workflow rather than hardware-independent speed benchmarks.

Results are organized by the three research questions stated in the Introduction. Figure 4 gives the selected empirical-realism checks, @tbl-method-overall and Figure 5 summarize structural recovery, Figure 6 isolates simulated measurement-quality factors, and Figure 7 reports computational feasibility.

## Empirical Realism Results

The first result checks the calibrated LOMM realism panel against selected distributional, temporal, spectral, and effective-dimensionality signatures of the MAFW-derived classifier-output score panels. @fig-empirical-realism summarizes the check at two levels: the observed score channels and the recovered community-score summaries extracted from the pooled DynEGA solution. The figure is generated from the empirical-realism file `metric_comparison_long.csv`, not from the final dimensional-recovery simulation outputs. The check is limited to selected score-series similarities used for simulation construction; scoring-model validity and emotion-label validity require separate evidence.

```{r}
#| label: fig-empirical-realism
#| fig-cap: "Selected empirical-realism checks for the calibrated LOMM realism panel. Panel A shows pass, partial, and fail classifications for six score-series targets at observed-channel and recovered community-summary readouts. Panel B shows the two discrepancy components separately; dashed reference lines mark the pass threshold of 0.33 and fail threshold of 1.00."
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "0.98\\linewidth"
#| fig-pos: "H"

figure_4_path <- file.path("figures", "figure4_empirical_realism.pdf")
if (!file.exists(figure_4_path)) {
  figure_4_path <- file.path("paper", "figures", "figure4_empirical_realism.pdf")
}
knitr::include_graphics(figure_4_path)
```

At the observed-channel level, the calibrated realism panel passed the derivative-IQR and run-length entropy checks. Lag-1 autocorrelation, spectral entropy, and effective rank were partial score-series matches because they did not meet the strictest threshold. Channel IQR failed, showing that the simulated observed channels remained more dispersed than the empirical score channels. The softmax-linked panel is used for this realism check; the dimensional-recovery simulations use the linear block-measurement score panels described in the model section.

The recovered community-score summaries showed the same main boundary with a stronger amplitude mismatch. The community-score Channel IQR median was 0.832 in LOMM and 0.247 in the empirical panels, with a maximum scaled discrepancy of 1.481. This identifies amplitude dispersion as the main calibration boundary. The scenario construction is therefore usable for method testing, with amplitude dispersion retained as a calibration limit. The check does not establish empirical validity for the linear recovery panels.

The next analyses use the linear LOMM panels to evaluate known-truth recovery.

## Simulation Results

The recovery analysis separates scalability, direct method comparison, simulated measurement-quality sensitivity, and computational feasibility. DynEGA was evaluated on the broad Louvain/expand grid and on the matched four-indicator design shared with GraphicalVAR and GIMME. The matched comparison aggregates across Louvain, Leiden, and Walktrap readouts and treats community detection as a diagnostic factor. @tbl-method-overall summarizes dimensional recovery, status counts, assignment accuracy, and successful-fit runtime by method.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-method-overall
#| tbl-cap: "Overall method behavior in the final matched four-indicator grid, aggregated across Louvain, Leiden, and Walktrap readouts. Rows are method-community-detection readout rows. Hit rate is recovery of the generating number of latent dimensions using all readout rows as the denominator; Assignment is optimal block-assignment accuracy for readouts with available partitions. Median runtime is computed over successful fitted structures."
#| results: asis

method_table_path <- file.path("tables", "table1_method_overall.csv")
if (!file.exists(method_table_path)) {
  method_table_path <- file.path("paper", "tables", "table1_method_overall.csv")
}
method_table <- readr::read_csv(method_table_path, show_col_types = FALSE)
method_table_display <- method_table |>
  dplyr::select(Method, Rows, ok, timeout, error, `Hit (%)`, `Assign. (%)`, `Runtime (s)`) |>
  dplyr::rename(
    `Total rows` = Rows,
    `Valid rows` = ok,
    Timeouts = timeout,
    Errors = error,
    `Assignment (%)` = `Assign. (%)`,
    `Median runtime (s)` = `Runtime (s)`
  )
cat("\\begingroup\\scriptsize\\setlength{\\tabcolsep}{3pt}\n")
print(knitr::kable(
  method_table_display,
  booktabs = TRUE,
  align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r")
))
cat("\\endgroup\n")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-dimension-recovery
#| fig-cap: "Dimensional hit rate across the final matched four-indicator method-comparison conditions. Lines show methods and vertical intervals show cluster-bootstrap 95% confidence intervals, resampling generated panels while retaining their community-detection readouts. Condition codes A--F refer to the simulated score-panel regimes in @tbl-scenario-families. Hit rates are status-inclusive and aggregated across Louvain, Leiden, and Walktrap readouts."
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "0.98\\linewidth"
#| fig-pos: "H"

figure_5_path <- file.path("figures", "figure5_dimension_recovery.pdf")
if (!file.exists(figure_5_path)) {
  figure_5_path <- file.path("paper", "figures", "figure5_dimension_recovery.pdf")
}
knitr::include_graphics(figure_5_path)
```

DynEGA was the only method evaluated on the broad grid and completed all 518,400 Louvain/expand rows. On that grid, it recovered the generating number of dimensions in 93.7% of rows and assigned observed classifier-output channels to the generating blocks with 95.2% accuracy. @tbl-method-overall reports status-inclusive method-readout rows after community-detection readouts. Unique structure-fit feasibility counts are reported in the Computational Feasibility section and Appendix D. Aggregating across Louvain, Leiden, and Walktrap, DynEGA recovered the generating number of dimensions in 95.3% of matched-grid rows, GraphicalVAR in 80.3%, and GIMME in 25.9%. Assignment accuracy followed the same ordering among readouts with available partitions: 96.0% for DynEGA, 90.4% for GraphicalVAR, and 67.2% for GIMME.

@fig-dimension-recovery shows the matched-grid scenario pattern. DynEGA retained the strongest recovery profile across the simulated score-panel regimes. GraphicalVAR recovered the generating dimensionality in many ranked-persistence and broad-switching-geometry conditions when the structure fit completed, while recovery dropped in the low-expression single-dominance condition. GIMME showed the lowest status-inclusive recovery because many fits timed out or produced no usable contemporaneous structure for partitioning.

Because method and generated scenario family dominated dimensional hit rate, @fig-factor-effects isolates the simulated measurement-quality factors that directly alter the observed score panels. The descriptive row-level factor screen showed the same ordering: method and scenario family had the largest associations with dimensional hit rate, measurement-error standard deviation also mattered, loading strength had a smaller association, and community detection contributed essentially no variation. These effect-size summaries are descriptive because community-detection readouts from the same fitted structure are repeated in the row-level data.

```{r}
#| label: fig-factor-effects
#| fig-cap: "Dimensional hit rate stratified by measurement-error standard deviation and loading strength in the final matched four-indicator grid. Columns show loading strength; lines and symbols show methods. Hit rates are status-inclusive. Error bars are descriptive Wilson intervals computed from method-readout rows in each stratum, aggregated across community-detection readouts."
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "0.98\\linewidth"
#| fig-pos: "H"

figure_6_path <- file.path("figures", "figure6_factor_effects.pdf")
if (!file.exists(figure_6_path)) {
  figure_6_path <- file.path("paper", "figures", "figure6_factor_effects.pdf")
}
knitr::include_graphics(figure_6_path)
```

@fig-factor-effects shows how method differences changed across measurement quality. DynEGA was most stable across the loading-by-error grid, although low-signal scenarios still reduced recovery. GraphicalVAR was more sensitive to the measurement layer: its hit rate was weakest when loadings were low and measurement error was high, and improved when observed channels carried a stronger signal from their generating dimensions. GIMME remained lower on status-inclusive hit rate across most strata because errors and timeouts occurred before dimensional recovery could be evaluated. This loading-by-error gradient tracks the population signal-to-noise ratio $\lambda^2 V/\psi$ that drives both graph readouts in Appendix A.

Conditional on obtaining a usable structural readout, trajectory-recovery diagnostics followed the same measurement pattern. Recovery was strongest in the ranked-persistence and broad switching-geometry generated regimes and deteriorated as measurement-error standard deviation increased. These diagnostics are conditional summaries, not status-inclusive method-performance measures; full marginal means are reported in Appendix C.

## Computational Feasibility

Computational feasibility was evaluated separately from recovery accuracy because the methods differed in both recovery behavior and scalability across the simulation design. @fig-runtime-feasibility summarizes successful-fit runtime in the matched four-indicator grid, and the text below accounts for broad-grid completion, timeouts, and post-estimation errors. This distinction is important for interpreting the comparator results: GraphicalVAR and GIMME are informative matched-grid comparisons with more limited scalability across the full LOMM grid.

```{r}
#| label: fig-runtime-feasibility
#| fig-cap: "Runtime of the compared methods in the final matched four-indicator grid. The y-axis is shown on a log10 time scale. Points show median runtime for successful fitted structures and intervals show the interquartile range. For GraphicalVAR and GIMME, the same fitted structure is reused across Louvain, Leiden, and Walktrap readouts."
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "0.98\\linewidth"
#| fig-pos: "H"

figure_7_path <- file.path("figures", "figure7_runtime_feasibility.pdf")
if (!file.exists(figure_7_path)) {
  figure_7_path <- file.path("paper", "figures", "figure7_runtime_feasibility.pdf")
}
knitr::include_graphics(figure_7_path)
```

DynEGA was substantially faster than the two model-based comparators in the matched design. Median successful-fit runtime was 2.61 s for DynEGA, compared with 86.1 s for GraphicalVAR and 280.5 s for GIMME. The broad DynEGA Louvain/expand grid also completed all 518,400 method rows without errors or timeouts. GraphicalVAR completed 20,872 of 21,600 matched-grid structure fits and timed out on 728 fits. GIMME completed 15,294 of 21,600 matched-grid structure fits, timed out on 4,114 fits, and returned post-estimation errors for 2,192 fits. Because GraphicalVAR and GIMME apply three community-detection algorithms to each fitted structure, these feasibility counts refer to unique structure fits before repeated CD readouts; Appendix D reports the fit-level and readout-row accounting side by side. In these LOMM simulation designs, DynEGA combined the strongest structural recovery with broad-grid scalability, GraphicalVAR was informative but slower and more condition-sensitive, and GIMME was feasibility-limited.

# Discussion

<!-- REVISION_RESULTS_PENDING[integrate_manuscript]; CLAIM_LEDGER[clm-v2-held-out-realism,clm-v2-matched-recovery,clm-v2-short-record,clm-v2-measurement-challenges,clm-v2-runtime-feasibility]: Retain the checked-in quantitative interpretation until every required revision job is COMPLETE and the aggregate result contract validates. -->

LOMM gave a controlled score-generation problem for evaluating dynamic dimensional recovery. The empirical-realism checks reproduced local movement and directional-change texture, partially matched persistence, spectral complexity, and effective multivariate dimensionality, and retained a clear amplitude-dispersion mismatch. In the recovery grids, DynEGA recovered the generating dimensionality and indicator blocks most consistently in these LOMM simulation designs and completed the broad focal-method grid. Recovery weakened when simulated measurement signal was lower. GraphicalVAR was informative but condition-sensitive, and GIMME was feasibility-limited in the matched design. The trajectory-recovery diagnostics add a conditional result among method-readout rows with recovered score summaries; they are not a status-inclusive method ranking.

Appendix A frames recovery in the linear panels as a method-specific graph perturbation problem. Under the linear LOMM measurement model, indicators assigned to the same latent oscillator share a common change signal. Indicators assigned to different oscillators are independent. The measurement signal within each dimension is rank-one, and per-channel filtered population graphs form disconnected weighted cliques under the symmetric block target. DynEGA reads this structure through smoothed derivative estimates. GraphicalVAR reaches the same block algebra through a multivariate VAR innovation projection under the simplified population target. GIMME adds an indirect graph-conversion and completion layer rather than a closed-form population block edge. The population edge sets how much common block signal reaches community detection, and recovery becomes more difficult when the method-specific perturbation approaches the weakest within-block edge.

DynEGA is closely aligned with this target in these LOMM simulation designs. DynEGA groups variables whose estimated changes are coordinated over time, so the common derivative signal within each LOMM block is the relevant recovery signal. The high dimensional hit rate, high block-assignment accuracy, and complete broad-grid coverage indicate that this signal usually remained identifiable across the simulated score-panel regimes. The reductions under weak loadings, high measurement error, and low-expression generated regimes identify conditions in which the observed channels no longer carry enough common dynamic variation for reliable partitioning.

The generator separates three parts of the measurement problem. The oscillator layer controls restoring forces, momentum, and stochastic perturbation. The activity layer controls dominance and switching. The measurement layer controls indicator strength and error before scores are placed on their observed scale for empirical-realism checks. This separation lets method researchers test whether an analysis recovers latent organization or responds mainly to features of the observation system.

GraphicalVAR represents the generating measurement blocks less directly. In this comparison, community detection is applied to the contemporaneous partial-correlation matrix, which conditions each pairwise association on the remaining channels. Appendix A shows that, in the symmetric block model, the population VAR innovation graph preserves block support but compresses the within-block edge toward a ceiling set by block size. The VAR projection also removes the predictable part of the common block signal before the contemporaneous graph is read. The observed sensitivity of GraphicalVAR is consistent with this mechanism, especially when loadings are weak or measurement error is high. The simulation does not isolate this population attenuation from lag estimation, regularization, finite-sample variation, or timeout behavior. In the matched grid, GraphicalVAR completed most structure fits and had 728 unique structure-fit timeouts, so its main limitation in this comparison was condition sensitivity with some timeout loss.

GIMME has broader native aims than dimensional partitioning. It searches for group, subgroup, and individual lagged and contemporaneous paths. In the present evaluation, video clips are analytic time series; clip-specific contemporaneous structures are averaged and then partitioned with a separate community-detection step. Its lower status-inclusive hit rate therefore reflects both the indirect GIMME-to-community graph and substantial feasibility costs, including long successful-fit runtimes, timeouts, and post-estimation errors. The result evaluates the implemented clip-level GIMME-to-community procedure under this design. Person-level idiographic applications of GIMME require separate evidence.

With a valid structural graph, trajectory-recovery diagnostics showed the largest marginal differences by generated scenario family and measurement-error standard deviation. Ranked-persistence and broad switching-geometry panels produced the closest trajectory summaries. Low-expression single-dominance panels were the most difficult. These diagnostics evaluate recovery of simulated latent trajectories after a usable structure has been estimated. They do not evaluate classifier-output validity, emotion-label validity, or status-inclusive method performance. Full marginal summaries are reported in Appendix C.

The empirical realism check limits the interpretation to selected statistical resemblance between simulated panels and classifier-output score panels from the MAFW calibration sample. The check cannot validate the scoring model, the prompt labels, or subjective emotional states in the videos. The calibration used one dataset label schema and one scoring implementation, and the empirical clips were short relative to some simulation regimes. The short empirical clips support calibration of selected local score-series properties. The longer simulation conditions test method behavior under controlled series lengths. The current softmax-linked realism panel reproduces several local temporal and effective-dimensionality features, while amplitude dispersion remains in the large descriptive-discrepancy band.

The comparison is narrow by design. The method-comparison results apply to the linear block-measurement recovery panels, and the softmax-linked panels were used for empirical-realism calibration. The present LOMM implementation uses independent oscillator dimensions, activity-gated block loadings, and diagonal measurement error. These choices make the recovery target interpretable, but they simplify the geometry of visible expressive behavior and the dependence structure of classifier-output score channels. The method comparison covers network-based or network-convertible recovery pipelines. Other dynamic latent-variable approaches remain outside the present evaluation. Future work should test richer oscillator coupling, cross-loadings, correlated measurement error, alternative bounded or compositional observation layers, additional scoring systems, and empirical applications where simulation results guide method validation before substantive interpretation of classifier-output score dynamics. The present results support LOMM as a controlled validation environment for selected temporal and dimensional properties. Full generative theories of affect and validation of scoring-model emotion labels require separate evidence.
