# Appendix A: Perturbation Targets for LOMM Recovery

Appendix A explains why the same block-measured linear panel gives different recovery margins for DynEGA, GraphicalVAR, and GIMME. The linear panel can be written as a graph perturbation problem: each method supplies a population structural signal for the same score panel, and implementation adds finite-sample, estimation, convergence, extraction, and community-detection perturbations.

The argument has three claims. First, idealized DynEGA and GraphicalVAR population graphs preserve the generating block support exactly under the symmetric linear block target. Second, their within-block partial-correlation edges share one ceiling; their difference comes from the signal-to-noise ratio delivered by derivative or VAR innovation filtering. Third, GIMME has a different mathematical status because recovery depends on path search, convergence, extraction, averaging, graph conversion, and completion. The sections below define the target, derive the two population graph maps, state the perturbation margin, and summarize the method comparison.

| Result or layer | Main assumptions | Planned departures and interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| Exact block support | Mutually independent latent factors, one primary loading per indicator, and independent measurement errors | Cross-loadings, correlated residuals, and correlated shocks test how cross-block edges erode separation |
| Per-channel filter invariance | The same linear temporal filter is applied to every indicator, with boundary handling fixed | Short records, embedding selection, and gate transitions can change finite-sample filter behavior |
| Within-block edge formula | Exchangeable loadings and error variances within a block, with positive filtered signal variance | Loading and variance jitter perturb edge equality while preserving the ideal support target |
| Connected-component recovery | The weakest population within-block edge exceeds the total graph perturbation | Regularization, sampling error, estimation failure, and community detection contribute to the perturbation |
| GIMME recovery decomposition | A usable contemporaneous graph can be extracted and partitioned | Convergence, timeout, extraction, symmetrization, and completion are separate parts of the pipeline estimand |

: Assumptions behind the Appendix A population results and the prespecified revision challenges. {#tbl-lomm-assumptions}

## A.1 Linear Block Target

Consider a population LOMM with $m$ latent dimensions, $k$ observed indicators per dimension, and $p=mk$ observed score channels. Let $B_1,\ldots,B_m$ denote the true indicator blocks. For indicator $j \in B_f$, use the equal-loading, equal-error measurement model

$$
Y_j(t)=\lambda Z_f(t)+\varepsilon_j(t),
\qquad
Z_f(t)=a_f(t)X_f(t),
$$

where $Z_f(t)$ is the activity-scaled latent oscillator for dimension $f$, $\lambda>0$, and $\varepsilon_j(t)$ is measurement error with variance $\psi=s_\varepsilon^2$. Measurement errors are independent across indicators and time in this target, so $\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_j(t),\varepsilon_\ell(s))=0$ whenever $j\neq \ell$ or $t\neq s$. The latent processes $Z_f$ are zero-mean and mutually independent in this simplified population object. Activity gating makes $Z_f$ nonstationary by design, so the variances used in this appendix are time-averaged second moments over the analyzed window. Loading jitter, item-level variance jitter, switching schedules, initialization transients, finite-sample activity imbalance, and estimator behavior are treated as perturbations around this symmetric target.

For a method readout $r$, write the fitted graph as

$$
\widehat{\mathbf{W}}^{(r)}
=
\mathbf{W}_*^{(r)}+\mathbf{E}^{(r)}.
$$

Here $\mathbf{W}_*^{(r)}$ is the population structural matrix induced by the method readout, and $\mathbf{E}^{(r)}$ collects finite-sample variation, derivative estimation, model estimation, regularization, convergence behavior, extraction errors, and community-detection effects. This notation keeps the comparison focused on two quantities: the population signal available to the method and the perturbation added by the implemented pipeline.

## A.2 Filtered Panels and Two Graph Readouts

The derivation uses two population graph maps for a per-channel filtered block panel. DynEGA estimates local derivatives of every channel, and a lag difference is a simple analytic example of the same channelwise operation. GraphicalVAR is handled separately in A.3 because its contemporaneous innovations come from a multivariate VAR projection rather than from an identical filter applied to each channel.

Let $L$ denote a linear filter applied to each channel separately. Applying $L$ to the measurement model for $j \in B_f$ gives

$$
(LY_j)(t)=\lambda\,(LZ_f)(t)+(L\varepsilon_j)(t),
$$

so the filtered panel keeps the one-factor block structure. Write $V_{L,f}=\operatorname{Var}(LZ_f)$ for the filtered common-signal variance and $\psi_L=\operatorname{Var}(L\varepsilon_j)$ for the filtered noise variance. Because $L$ acts on each channel separately, filtered errors stay independent across channels, and the within-block covariance matrix of the filtered channels is

$$
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{L,f}
=
\lambda^{2}V_{L,f}\,\mathbf{1}_k\mathbf{1}_k^\top+\psi_L I_k,
\qquad
\theta_{L,f}=\frac{\lambda^{2}V_{L,f}}{\psi_L},
$$

with zero cross-block covariance. The filtered signal-to-noise ratio $\theta_{L,f}$ is the only quantity through which the filter enters the population graph. Filtered errors can be serially correlated; the population readouts below use only the contemporaneous covariance across channels, and serial dependence is absorbed into the estimation perturbation in A.4.

The filtered panel admits two graph readouts. The marginal readout uses correlations directly. For two distinct indicators $j,\ell \in B_f$,

$$
w^{M}_f(L)
=
\left|\operatorname{Cor}(LY_j,LY_\ell)\right|
=
\frac{\theta_{L,f}}{1+\theta_{L,f}}.
$$

The partial readout conditions each pair on the remaining channels. Using the Sherman-Morrison identity,

$$
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{L,f}^{-1}
=
\psi_L^{-1}
\left[
I_k-
\frac{\theta_{L,f}}{1+k\theta_{L,f}}
\mathbf{1}_k\mathbf{1}_k^\top
\right],
$$

and the absolute partial correlation between two indicators in the same block is

$$
w^{P}_f(L)
=
\frac{\theta_{L,f}}{1+(k-1)\theta_{L,f}}.
$$

Because the filtered precision matrix is block-diagonal, cross-block partial correlations are exactly zero. These marginal and partial readouts therefore preserve the generating block support without error for the per-channel filtered population object, and the population graph has block-clique form for any per-channel filter,

$$
\mathbf{W}_*
=
\operatorname{blockdiag}
\left(
w_1(J_k-I_k),\ldots,w_m(J_k-I_k)
\right),
\qquad
w_f\in\{w^{M}_f(L),\,w^{P}_f(L)\}.
$$

The two readouts differ in how much within-block signal they keep. For the same signal-to-noise ratio $\theta$,

$$
\frac{w^P(\theta)}{w^M(\theta)}
=
\frac{1+\theta}{1+(k-1)\theta},
$$

so $w^P(\theta)<w^M(\theta)$ whenever $k>2$ and $\theta>0$. As $\theta \to \infty$,

$$
w^P(\theta)\to \frac{1}{k-1},
\qquad
w^M(\theta)\to 1.
$$

The partial readout compresses an arbitrarily strong common-source signal toward a ceiling set by block size alone: with four indicators per dimension, no within-block partial-correlation edge can exceed $1/3$. Both readout maps are increasing in $\theta$, so filter and readout separate cleanly. The filter sets $\theta_{L,f}$, and the readout maps $\theta_{L,f}$ to the edge weight supplied to community detection.

@fig-readout-curves compares the marginal and partial maps for the matched grid's four indicators per dimension. The marginal map is a pre-conditioning benchmark; neither implemented pipeline uses it. The vertical gap between the curves shows how much compression the partial map applies to the common-source signal. The shaded band marks the $\lambda^2/s_\varepsilon^2$ span of the matched measurement grid, so the simulated loading and error conditions place $\theta_{L,f}$ inside the band up to the filtered common-signal variance $V_{L,f}$. Across that span, the marginal curve rises from mid-range values toward 1. The partial curve is already near its $1/3$ ceiling: strong measurement conditions widen the common-source signal margin but cannot widen the partial-correlation edge beyond the ceiling.

```{r}
#| label: fig-readout-curves
#| fig-cap: "Population within-block edge weight as a function of the filtered signal-to-noise ratio for the marginal and partial readouts with four indicators per dimension. The dotted line marks the partial-readout ceiling $1/(k-1)=1/3$. The shaded band spans the loading-to-error-variance ratios of the matched simulation grid; the filtered common-signal variance multiplies the signal-to-noise ratio within this band. Higher edge weight means more within-block signal margin before estimation perturbations."
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "0.9\\linewidth"
#| fig-pos: "H"

readout_curves_path <- file.path("figures", "perturbation_readout_curves.pdf")
if (!file.exists(readout_curves_path)) {
  readout_curves_path <- file.path("paper", "figures", "perturbation_readout_curves.pdf")
}
knitr::include_graphics(readout_curves_path)
```

## A.3 Method-Specific Filters and Signal-to-Noise Ratios

The implemented pipelines are specific readout combinations. DynEGA estimates generalized local linear approximation (GLLA) derivatives of each score channel over a time-delay embedding window and then estimates a regularized partial-correlation network (EBICglasso) on the derivative panel. The implementation uses one observation interval as the GLLA `delta` and retains the generator's physical $dt=0.4$ in separate horizon metadata. Conversion to physical-time derivatives applies the same positive scale factor to every channel and therefore leaves the derivative correlation readout unchanged. DynEGA's population object is the partial readout of a per-channel derivative filter, $w^{P}_f(L_{\mathrm{GLLA}})$. A lag-$h$ difference, $\Delta_hY_j(t)=Y_j(t+h)-Y_j(t)$, gives a transparent analytic stand-in for that filter, with

$$
\theta^{\Delta}_f
=
\frac{\lambda^2\operatorname{Var}(\Delta_hZ_f)}{2\psi},
$$

because independent measurement errors contribute $2\psi$ to the variance of every differenced channel. Both the lag difference and GLLA derivative estimation operate channel by channel. For the smooth oscillator trajectories generated here, the GLLA filter improves on this stand-in: it averages frame-level measurement noise over the embedding window while tracking the common latent change signal, which supports a high filtered signal-to-noise ratio.

GraphicalVAR reads partial correlations from the contemporaneous innovations of a lag-1 vector autoregression, so its population object is the partial readout of a multivariate VAR innovation projection, $w^{P}_f(L_{\mathrm{VAR}})$. For the population lag-1 fit of the symmetric block model, the implied coefficient matrix is proportional to $\mathbf{1}_k\mathbf{1}_k^\top$ within each block, and the innovation covariance retains the one-factor-plus-diagonal form. The compression map of A.2 therefore applies at the innovation scale under this symmetric target. The VAR projection also removes the predictable part of the common signal by construction: the simulated oscillator trajectories are strongly autocorrelated, so the lagged panel explains much of the common variance, while the serially independent measurement error passes into the innovations. The innovation readout therefore tends to enter the shared compression map with a smaller signal-to-noise ratio than a derivative filter applied to the same panel.

The population comparison between DynEGA and GraphicalVAR then has a precise form. Both population readouts supply partial-correlation edges to community detection, so both within-block edges are capped at $1/(k-1)$ and the generating block support is preserved in both population objects under the symmetric target. The population difference is where the derivative and innovation signal-to-noise ratios $\theta_{\mathrm{GLLA}}$ and $\theta_{\mathrm{VAR}}$ place each edge below that shared ceiling. The remaining differences are pipeline perturbations, which A.4 collects in a single margin.

## A.4 Shared Perturbation Margin

Let a method's population graph have block-clique form

$$
\mathbf{W}_*^{(r)}
=
\operatorname{blockdiag}
\left(
w_1^{(r)}(J_k-I_k),\ldots,w_m^{(r)}(J_k-I_k)
\right),
$$

where edge weights are on the nonnegative scale supplied to community detection and all $m$ blocks share the same size $k$. For DynEGA and GraphicalVAR, $w_f^{(r)}=w^{P}_f(L_r)$ with the method-specific filter from A.3. Suppose every off-diagonal edge is estimated within $\delta_r$ of its readout-specific population value:

$$
\max_{j\neq \ell}
\left|
\widehat{W}^{(r)}_{j\ell}-W^{(r)}_{*,j\ell}
\right|
\leq \delta_r.
$$

For any node $j \in B_f$, the estimated total connection to its true block is at least

$$
(k-1)(w_f^{(r)}-\delta_r),
$$

whereas its estimated total connection to any wrong block is at most

$$
k\delta_r.
$$

Thus each node has stronger total connection to its true block than to any wrong block whenever

$$
(k-1)(w_{\min}^{(r)}-\delta_r)>k\delta_r,
$$

or equivalently

$$
\delta_r
<
\frac{k-1}{2k-1}w_{\min}^{(r)}.
$$

For the matched grid with $k=4$, the sufficient node-level block-preference and threshold-separation condition is

$$
\delta_r < \frac{3}{7}w_{\min}^{(r)}.
$$

This margin is not a guarantee that Louvain, Leiden, or Walktrap recover the blocks, because exact recovery depends on the implemented community-detection algorithm. The bound has a narrower consequence. Because $\tfrac{k-1}{2k-1}<\tfrac{1}{2}$, the condition forces every estimated cross-block edge below every estimated within-block edge, so any threshold $\tau\in(\delta_r,\,w_{\min}^{(r)}-\delta_r)$ deletes all cross-block edges, keeps each block a connected clique, and reproduces the generating blocks exactly as the connected components of the thresholded graph.

The margin treats perturbation as symmetric noise on every edge, which makes $\delta_r$ a worst-case envelope. Regularized estimation acts asymmetrically: glasso shrinkage lowers within-block edges, which reduces $w_{\min}^{(r)}$, and sets weak cross-block edges to zero, which supports block separation.

The two population partial-readout pipelines share the same ceiling. DynEGA and GraphicalVAR supply partial-correlation edges to community detection, so $w_{\min}^{(r)}\leq 1/(k-1)$ for both pipelines, and with $k=4$ the sufficient perturbation margin approaches at most

$$
\delta_r
<
\frac{3}{7}\cdot\frac{1}{3}
=
\frac{1}{7}
$$

in the high-signal limit. The population comparison therefore reduces to the two quantities identified in A.3: how close each filtered signal-to-noise ratio keeps $w_{\min}^{(r)}$ to the shared ceiling, and how large each pipeline's realized perturbation $\delta_r$ is. The observed recovery ordering is consistent with the derivative filter preserving more within-block signal than the innovation filter. The full graphical vector-autoregression fit also adds larger estimation and timeout perturbations.

The margin also identifies which blocks are fragile in each scenario family. Activity gating enters the filtered signal directly: $V_{L,f}$ is the time-averaged variance of the filtered activity-scaled process, so a dimension held at background gain contributes a small $\theta_{L,f}$ and a weak within-block edge. In the single-dominance families, background dimensions run at gains of 0.05--0.08 against active gains of 0.35--1.25 (Appendix E), so $w_{\min}^{(r)}$ is set by the background blocks, and in the low-expression family every dimension sits near background activity. The margin therefore predicts the scenario-family ordering observed in @fig-dimension-recovery for DynEGA and GraphicalVAR: recovery is hardest where the activity schedule holds the weakest block's signal lowest. For GIMME, the same activity envelope is an expected stressor, but its effect is mediated by path search, convergence, extraction, averaging, graph conversion, and completion.

## A.5 GIMME as an Indirect Graph-Conversion Readout

The implemented GIMME comparator has a different mathematical status. Its readout can be summarized as

$$
\widehat{\mathbf{W}}^G
=
\Pi
\left(
\frac{1}{V}\sum_{i=1}^{V}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_i
\right),
$$

where $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_i$ is the clip-specific contemporaneous structure extracted from GIMME for clip $i$, $V$ is the number of clips, and $\Pi(\cdot)$ denotes conversion to the undirected graph supplied to community detection. This readout depends on path search, clip-level model selection, convergence, extraction, averaging, and graph conversion. We therefore summarize GIMME as an indirect graph-conversion pipeline without a closed-form block edge $w_f^G$.

Status-inclusive recovery also includes completion. For any pipeline,

$$
\Pr(\mathrm{hit})
=
\Pr(\mathrm{usable\ graph})
\Pr(\mathrm{hit}\mid \mathrm{usable\ graph}).
$$

The reported feasibility tables make this decomposition concrete. DynEGA returned usable graphs for every broad-grid and matched-grid row, so its status-inclusive and conditional hit rates coincide at 95.3%. GraphicalVAR completed 20,872 of 21,600 matched-grid structure fits (62,616 of 64,800 readout rows), so its 80.3% status-inclusive hit rate corresponds to a conditional hit rate of about 83% among usable readouts. GIMME completed 15,294 of 21,600 structure fits (45,882 of 64,800 readout rows), so its 25.9% status-inclusive hit rate corresponds to a conditional hit rate of about 37%. The decomposition separates GIMME's two losses: many fits return no usable graph, and partition quality after a usable graph remains well below the other pipelines.

  "GraphicalVAR", "$w^P(\\theta_{\\mathrm{VAR}})$: partial readout of VAR innovations", "VAR estimation, regularization, innovation-projection attenuation, timeouts", "Population VAR innovation readout preserves block support under the symmetric block target",
  "GIMME", "No closed-form block signal for the implemented readout", "Path search, clip-level fitting, extraction, averaging, timeouts", "Indirect feasibility-stress comparator"
)

  runtime_accounting_path <- file.path("paper", "tables", "table3_runtime_feasibility_accounting.csv")
}

  dplyr::select(

# Appendix E: Supplementary Scenario Parameter Values

The final scenario families use the numeric settings below. The reported final runs fix the quality scale at $Q=0.75$. The base $\sigma_q$ vectors in the numeric dynamic-vector table are therefore the final-run innovation vectors, applied as per-step shock standard deviations at the step size used for each series length ($dt=0.4$ for 100-point series and $dt=0.25$ for 300-point series). The simulation code also supports configurable reruns with $\sigma_q=\text{scenario base }\sigma_q\times(Q/0.75)$.

Codes A--D use asymptotically stable template feedback. Codes E--F use ranked feedback with $\eta_f<0$ and $\zeta_f>0$, which produces finite-horizon anti-damped oscillations. Their interpretation is restricted to the reported observation horizons. The prospective empirical realism calibration compares unconstrained and stable negative-$\zeta$ grids; it does not alter these checked-in scenario parameters.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-scenario-schedule-supplement
#| results: asis

fmt_vec <- function(x) paste(sprintf("%.2f", x), collapse = "; ")
dimensions <- 2:4
template_eta <- c(-0.30, -0.55, -0.85, -1.10)
template_zeta <- c(-1.70, -1.00, -0.65, -0.30)
template_sigma <- c(0.12, 0.30, 0.45, 0.65)
ranked_eta <- -0.05 * seq_len(4)
ranked_zeta <- 0.06 + 0.02 * seq_len(4)

scenario_schedule_table <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Code, ~Family, ~Source, ~Switching, ~Gain, ~Dwell, ~`Feedback source`,
  "A", "Low-expression single dominance", "Generic", "No", "0.35 / 0.05", "1.00 / 1.00", "Template",
  "B", "High-expression single dominance", "Generic", "No", "1.00 / 0.08", "1.00 / 1.00", "Template",
  "C", "High-expression switching", "Generic", "Yes", "1.00 / 0.08", "0.20 / 0.45", "Template",
  "D", "High-expression rapid switching", "Generic", "Yes", "1.25 / 0.08", "0.03 / 0.10", "Template",
  "E", "Ranked-persistence", "Calibration-inspired", "No", "1.00 / 0.08", "1.00 / 1.00", "Ranked",
  "F", "Broad switching-geometry", "Calibration-inspired", "Yes", "1.10 / 0.10", "0.12 / 0.30", "Ranked"
)

make_dynamic_rows <- function(code, eta, zeta, sigma_base) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(dimensions, function(dimension) {
    data.frame(
      Code = code,
      Dimensions = paste0(dimension, "D"),
      eta = fmt_vec(eta[seq_len(dimension)]),
      zeta = fmt_vec(zeta[seq_len(dimension)]),
      `Base sigma-q` = fmt_vec(sigma_base[seq_len(dimension)]),
      check.names = FALSE
    )
  }))
}

scenario_dynamic_table <- do.call(rbind, list(
  make_dynamic_rows("A", template_eta, template_zeta, template_sigma * 0.50),
  make_dynamic_rows("B", template_eta, template_zeta, template_sigma),
  make_dynamic_rows("C", template_eta, template_zeta, template_sigma),
  make_dynamic_rows("D", template_eta, template_zeta, template_sigma * 1.25),
  make_dynamic_rows("E", ranked_eta, ranked_zeta, rep(0.25, 4)),
  make_dynamic_rows("F", ranked_eta, ranked_zeta, rep(0.35, 4))
))

cat("\\begingroup\\scriptsize\\setlength{\\tabcolsep}{3pt}\n")
print(knitr::kable(
  scenario_schedule_table,
  format = "latex",
  longtable = TRUE,
  caption = "Scenario schedule and feedback-source settings for the final simulation families.",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  escape = FALSE,
  align = c("c", "p{1.75in}", "p{0.85in}", "c", "c", "c", "p{0.75in}")
))
cat("\\endgroup\n\n")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-scenario-stability-supplement
#| results: asis

scenario_vectors <- list(
  A = list(eta = template_eta, zeta = template_zeta),
  B = list(eta = template_eta, zeta = template_zeta),
  C = list(eta = template_eta, zeta = template_zeta),
  D = list(eta = template_eta, zeta = template_zeta),
  E = list(eta = ranked_eta, zeta = ranked_zeta),
  F = list(eta = ranked_eta, zeta = ranked_zeta)
)

stability_rows <- list()
stability_row <- 1L
for (code in names(scenario_vectors)) {
  for (dimension in dimensions) {
    for (factor in seq_len(dimension)) {
      eta_value <- scenario_vectors[[code]]$eta[[factor]]
      zeta_value <- scenario_vectors[[code]]$zeta[[factor]]
      discriminant <- zeta_value^2 + 4 * eta_value
      root_values <- (
        zeta_value + c(-1, 1) * sqrt(as.complex(discriminant))
      ) / 2
      max_real_root <- max(Re(root_values))
      regime <- if (eta_value < 0 && zeta_value < 0) {
        if (discriminant < 0) "Stable oscillatory" else "Stable nonoscillatory"
      } else if (max_real_root > 0) {
        if (discriminant < 0) "Anti-damped oscillatory" else "Amplifying nonoscillatory"
      } else {
        "Marginal or mixed"
      }

      stability_rows[[stability_row]] <- data.frame(
        Code = code,
        Dimensions = paste0(dimension, "D"),
        Factor = factor,
        eta = eta_value,
        zeta = zeta_value,
        Discriminant = discriminant,
        `Max Re(root)` = max_real_root,
        `rho(Phi[.4])` = exp(0.4 * max_real_root),
        `rho(Phi[.25])` = exp(0.25 * max_real_root),
        `g(H[100])` = exp((100 - 1) * 0.4 * max_real_root),
        `g(H[300])` = exp((300 - 1) * 0.25 * max_real_root),
        Regime = regime,
        check.names = FALSE
      )
      stability_row <- stability_row + 1L
    }
  }
}
stability_table <- dplyr::bind_rows(stability_rows) |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 4)))

cat("\\begingroup\\tiny\\setlength{\\tabcolsep}{2pt}\n")
print(knitr::kable(
  stability_table,
  format = "latex",
  longtable = TRUE,
  caption = "Deterministic stability and finite-horizon growth diagnostics for every reported scenario factor. H[100] = 39.6 and H[300] = 74.75 under the retained time-step rules.",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  escape = FALSE,
  align = c("c", "c", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "l")
))
cat("\\endgroup\n")
```
